job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Chloe Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I'm in lectures for my master's in power systems engineering, then in the lab modelling load on a substation for my dissertation. Friday and Saturday nights I shelve books at the campus library for cash. I live in student housing with my friend Tamsin, and I cook the same pasta four nights a week because the loan payment comes out on the first and it's most of what I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a little. Every year there's a new miracle and then the rollout turns into a mess. At the library my friends are tired of hearing about it, so I'd just tell them to keep their bills paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's the best news for me, because my degree stays worth what I paid for it. But it doesn't fix the debt. I owe more than a year of a graduate salary and I have about two weeks of rent saved, and there are maybe four grid employers within a train ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the library shifts and send thirty applications to utilities and consultancies by spring. I'd ask Dr Okafor, my supervisor, to put my name to the substation people she knows. And I'd keep doing my derivations by hand, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, mostly. I'm relieved the world isn't flipping over, but the debt letters feel loud. I get a knot in my stomach on the first of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned only a handful of grid jobs near you. What happens if none of them comes through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd move, even though it scares me. I'd take a contractor job at a transformer plant two hours away before I'd take a call centre job. But my mother cleans offices and has a bad knee, and I'm the one who drives her to appointments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Does that worry you when you picture job interviews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. At an internship, an engineer asked if I used a chatbot to check my work, and when I said no he raised an eyebrow. I'd rather understand a protection relay from the maths than have a chatbot guess it for me. But if it becomes required I'll learn it slowly and resent it.

say: I'd tell friends the hype will fade and **real work** like keeping the grid running still needs trained people.
I'd say the loan system is the bigger scandal than any **chatbot**.
think: My degree keeps its value, but **debt** is the real threat, not AI.
With only about four grid employers nearby, one bad hiring year could leave me **stuck**.
do: Send **30 applications** to utilities and consultancies by spring.
Keep the **library shifts** while I finish the master's.
Ask Dr Okafor (my supervisor) to **introduce me** to substation engineers.
feel: **Tense** about the first-of-the-month loan payment, though glad the world isn't flipping over.
S0.quote: I'd rather understand a protection relay from the maths than have a chatbot guess it for me.
fieldNote: **Debt** and a thin cushion, not AI, drive her worry even in the mildest world.
Proud refusal of AI tools; she frames it as understanding, not fear.
Mother's bad knee ties her to the region and limits where she can move.

steps.text: Send 30 job applications to utilities and consultancies by spring
Keep the Friday and Saturday library shelving shifts
Cook cheap pasta meals and skip the student bar nights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the unions and the universities need to act now, because entry-level work is what gets cut first. Companies will call it efficiency, and the graduates are the ones who pay. I'd post that on the student union page and sign whatever petition goes round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job gets harder. The paperwork a junior does, like checking drawings, writing reports and filling in forecasts, is exactly what software eats. The utility I interned at, Eastgate Power, already stopped replacing a clerk who left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to jobs that need a person on site, like substations and commissioning, because a screen can't climb a pylon yet. I'd also join the engineers' union as a student member for six pounds a month, and I'd look at one short course on power-system software. I'd still avoid generative tools as long as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried and a bit angry. It feels like I did everything right, top marks and two internships, and the door is being narrowed anyway. I lie awake doing the maths on my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in a junior grid engineer's week do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forecasting reports, drawing checks and the monthly reports to the regulator. Those were the tasks my internship manager gave to the juniors to teach us, and now software can draft them in minutes. I'd be left with the site visits, which I like, but there are fewer of those jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd resent learning AI. What would make you do it anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a manager says no one gets hired without it, I'd do it, grumbling. A job pays the debt and a principle doesn't. I'd just want it taught properly in a classroom, with the rules and who is responsible when it gets something wrong.

say: I'd say **entry-level jobs** are what vanish first and companies should answer for it.
I'd push the student union to demand **regulation** and graduate hiring guarantees.
think: The junior tasks that taught me the trade, like checking drawings, are exactly what **software takes**.
I did everything right and the **door narrows** anyway, which makes me angry.
do: Aim for **site-based roles** in substations and commissioning that software can't do.
Join the engineers' **union** as a student member for a monthly fee.
Take one short course on **power-system software**, not chatbots.
feel: **Angry and worried**, lying awake over the loan arithmetic.
S1.quote: I did everything right, top marks and two internships, and the door is being narrowed anyway.
fieldNote: Blames **employers** and weak regulation, not the technology itself.
Turns to collective action and site-based work as her hedge.
Would accept AI only if a job requires it and rules are clear.

steps.text: Apply for substation commissioning jobs that need people on site
Join the engineers' union as a student member
Take a short course on power-system modelling software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs emergency rules, today, not after. Governments should slow it down until people have income and a say. I'd be at the union rally, probably holding a sign I made badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm finished before I start. My whole career is the thinking work, forecasting and design, and it's gone by 2028 while I still owe the loan. Robots for the hands-on side come three years later, so maybe substations are a refuge until about 2031, but I wouldn't bet my house on it, and I don't have a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra and work every shift the library will give me. I'd apply to every site job I can find, even in other regions, and call every council I know about training. And I'd talk to my mother about moving in with her to save rent, which she'd love and I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's a kind of grey panic where I can't plan past the next payment. I keep thinking of Tamsin and the others on my course who feel the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What goes through your head about your master's finishing in that window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether a master's still makes sense at that point, because I'd be paying more loan for a qualification that's about to be worth less. I'd probably finish it, because quitting with the debt already taken would be even worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible if it arrives this fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies and the people who write the rules. Not the researchers, mostly. The firms are racing for the money and the governments keep saying they'll look into it later.

say: I'd demand **emergency rules** and income support before the technology spreads any further.
I'd tell the rally that the **companies and governments** are racing while ordinary people carry the risk.
think: My forecasting and design skills could be **gone by 2028**, and the loan stays.
Substation work might give me **three extra years**, but I wouldn't count on it.
do: Pick up **every library shift** available and drop all extra spending.
Apply for **site jobs** in other regions and ask councils about retraining money.
Talk to my mother about **moving in** to save rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a grey panic that makes planning past the next payment hard.
S2.quote: My whole career is the thinking work, forecasting and design, and it's gone by 2028 while I still owe the loan.
fieldNote: First scenario where she sees her **own work** vanishing on a date she can't outrun.
Collective and political response comes before any personal plan.
Moving back in with her mother is a real option but one she dislikes.

steps.text: Work every library shift offered and cut all extras
Go to the union rally and write to the local councillor
Ask my mother if I can move in to save rent
Apply for site jobs in other regions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to fight for something, like a graduate income guarantee or a hiring quota. The union should be loud about it now. I'd tell my friends to join instead of just complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still worried but I can breathe. By 2031 I'd have the master's done, maybe two years on a grid job, and some savings. That's better odds than arriving in 2028 with nothing. Still, the debt would be there and the clerk-type jobs would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to land a graduate job at a utility this year and put a third of every pay cheque against the loan. I'd learn the hands-on side, the commissioning and the field testing, because that's where I'd get three more years. And I'd start a savings account with a fixed amount, even a small one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year one, but not calm. I'd feel like someone who knows there's a storm on the radar and has time to find a coat. I can still lose the coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years feels different to two. What would you do with those three extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them to build an actual cushion, six months of rent. Then if my thinking tasks go in 2031 I'm not starting from zero. I'd also ask Dr Okafor about a trade qualification, like a chartered engineer route that includes site experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel safer in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clear rules on who gets help if jobs go, and union deals for graduates that apply before the cuts, not after. And a loan that stops growing if you're out of work. I can't be the only one who thinks that's fair.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to win real protections if people organise now.
I'd tell friends to **join the union** instead of just complaining online.
think: Five years gives me a master's, a job and **some savings**, which is better odds than two.
My debt is still there, and the **desk tasks** will go in 2031.
do: Land a **utility job** this year and put a third of each pay cheque on the loan.
Train in **commissioning and field testing**, where hands-on work lasts longer.
Build **six months** of rent in savings.
feel: **Not calm**, but better: like seeing a storm coming with time to find a coat.
S3.quote: I'd feel like someone who knows there's a storm on the radar and has time to find a coat. I can still lose the coat.
fieldNote: The **extra time** moves her from panic to planning, but debt keeps her anxious.
Targets a specific protection: loans that pause when you have no work.
Leans on the union and field skills as insurance.

steps.text: Take a utility job and put a third of each cheque on the loan
Learn commissioning and field testing on site
Join the union and push for a graduate income guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. There's time to retrain people properly and to write rules, and the people in charge have no excuse. I'd still go to meetings and pester my councillor, because ten years is easy to waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about myself and nervous about my mother. I'd have maybe eight working years behind me before the thinking tasks go, and a few more on site. She's in her sixties by then and cleans offices, and nobody is planning for people like her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take the best utility job I can and clear the loan by about thirty-two. Then I'd save and train in a hands-on speciality, like substation protection, so I stay useful when robots come to the field around 2039. I'd also buy a small flat with the money I save instead of renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, which surprises me. Ten years feels like a normal career length, so I'd be allowed to plan. I'd still check the news too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still be worried about your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Absolutely. I'd keep the loan as the first thing to clear, because debt is the only thing that makes me feel I can't turn down a bad job. If I'm free of it by thirty-two I can choose where to live and what to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the loan change anything about how you'd use those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. I'd not be the same person who said no to every AI tool. In ten years I'd have to know how to check what a machine tells me, and I'd teach that to the new graduates, honestly.

say: I'd say **ten years** is time to retrain people properly and write rules, and leaders have no excuse.
I'd keep **pushing my councillor** so the time isn't wasted.
think: I feel okay for myself but **worried for my mother**, whom nobody is planning for.
If the loan is gone by 32, I can **choose** where to live and what to learn.
do: Finish the master's and take the **best utility job** available.
Clear the **loan by about 32** and save for a small flat.
Specialise in **substation protection** work that stays hands-on.
feel: **Hopeful**, which surprises me, though I'd still check the news too much.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a normal career length, so I'd be allowed to plan. I'd still check the news too much.
fieldNote: Even with a **decade**, her loan and her mother's future keep the mood from calming.
The first scenario where she admits she might eventually use AI tools.
Plans around being useful in a hands-on speciality.

steps.text: Take a utility job after the master's and clear the loan by 32
Train in substation protection, a hands-on speciality
Press my councillor for retraining plans for older workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one by far. It gives me no time and I'd still owe the loan. What would help is simple: pause the loan payments if you lose work, guarantee graduates a placement, and have the union at the table before the firms decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'm scared for other people. I am. If the graduate jobs go, my mother is still going to be cleaning offices, and nobody is making plans for her. I'd rather someone made one.

headlineQuote: If the graduate jobs go, my mother is still going to be cleaning offices, and nobody is making plans for her.
portrait: Chloe is a **24-year-old** top graduate in electrical engineering, now doing a master's in power systems with a heavy student loan.
She works library shifts and lives in student housing, with **no family money** and a mother who cleans offices.
She never uses AI tools, preferring to **understand things by hand**, and blames employers and weak regulation.
Her mood moves between **anxious** and alarmed, and only the two-year world truly frightens her.
She would turn to the union, site-based work and a possible move before any chatbot.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because there's no time and the loan keeps growing.
whatWouldHelp: **Paused loan payments**, a graduate job placement and a union seat before firms decide.
